about: Grove kits: the shields (which ports they have, and which pins each port uses) and the Grove modules students plug into them. Teachers can edit this file. A Grove cable has four wires: yellow (SIG, the signal), white (SIG2, a second signal most modules don't use), red (VCC, power) and black (GND). Each module's "sim" says how the simulator treats it (its behaviour, and its legs in Grove pin order: yellow, white, red, black); tools/grove_art.mjs draws the parts from this file.

base-shield.name: Grove Base Shield V2
base-shield.what: The Base Shield sits on top of your Arduino and gives it Grove ports. Each Grove module plugs into a port with one cable: no breadboard and no loose wires.
base-shield.fit: Line the Base Shield's pins up with the holes along both edges of your Arduino and press it straight down, gently and evenly, until it sits firmly.
base-shield.switch: Slide the little switch near the A0 port to 5V (5V is right for an Uno or a Mega).

base-hat.name: Grove Base Hat for Raspberry Pi
base-hat.what: The Base Hat sits on your Raspberry Pi's pins and gives it Grove ports. It replaces the breadboard: each module plugs in with one cable. It can also read analog sensors (like a knob or a light sensor), which a Raspberry Pi can't do by itself.
base-hat.fit: Turn the Pi off. Line the Base Hat's socket up with all 40 of the Pi's pins and press it straight down, gently and evenly.

grove-led.name: Grove LED
grove-led.what: A Grove LED is a small light on its own board. It already has its resistor, so it just plugs in.
grove-led.legs: No legs to worry about: the Grove cable only fits one way. The LED in the socket has a long leg (+); if you ever swap the LED, the long leg goes in the hole marked +.
grove-led.did_you_know: You can swap the LED in a Grove LED socket for any colour of 5mm LED.

grove-button.name: Grove Button
grove-button.what: A button you press. While it's pressed, its signal is HIGH. When you let go, it's LOW.
grove-button.legs: No legs: plug a Grove cable into it. Unlike a breadboard button, a Grove button reads HIGH when pressed (it has its own resistor), so use INPUT, not INPUT_PULLUP.
grove-button.did_you_know: Inside the button, a tiny metal dome clicks down and joins two contacts together.

grove-micro-switch.name: Grove Micro Switch
grove-micro-switch.what: A micro switch has a long metal lever. When something pushes the lever (like a bin lid closing), the switch clicks and its signal goes HIGH.
grove-micro-switch.legs: No legs: plug a Grove cable into it. It reads HIGH while the lever is pushed down.
grove-micro-switch.did_you_know: Micro switches are in computer mice, microwave doors and lift buttons. They can click millions of times.

grove-servo.name: Grove Servo
grove-servo.what: A servo is a small motor that turns to an angle you choose, from 0 to 180 degrees. It can open a lid or point a dial.
grove-servo.legs: The Grove servo has a Grove plug on its cable: plug it straight into a port. On a Raspberry Pi, use the PWM port.
grove-servo.did_you_know: A servo checks where it is many times a second and corrects itself, which is why it holds its angle.

grove-ultrasonic.name: Grove Ultrasonic Ranger
grove-ultrasonic.what: It measures distance with sound you can't hear: it sends out a click and times the echo. It works from about 3 cm to 3.5 m.
grove-ultrasonic.legs: One Grove cable. It uses a single pin to send the click and listen for the echo (a breadboard HC-SR04 needs two).
grove-ultrasonic.did_you_know: Bats and dolphins find their way with echoes in the same way.

grove-rotary.name: Grove Rotary Angle Sensor
grove-rotary.what: A knob (a potentiometer). Turning it changes the number your program reads, from 0 to the top of the scale.
grove-rotary.legs: One Grove cable into an analog port (A0 to A3 on an Arduino; A0, A2, A4 or A6 on a Pi's Base Hat).
grove-rotary.did_you_know: Volume knobs on speakers are often potentiometers just like this one.

grove-light.name: Grove Light Sensor
grove-light.what: It tells your program how bright it is. Brighter light gives a bigger number.
grove-light.legs: One Grove cable into an analog port.
grove-light.did_you_know: Street lights and phone screens use light sensors to switch on or dim by themselves.

grove-moisture.name: Grove Moisture Sensor
grove-moisture.what: Push its two prongs into soil. Wetter soil gives a bigger number, so you can tell when a plant needs water.
grove-moisture.legs: One Grove cable into an analog port. Only the prongs go in the soil, never the board or the cable.
grove-moisture.did_you_know: Water lets a little electricity flow between the prongs. Dry soil hardly lets any through.

grove-relay.name: Grove Relay
grove-relay.what: A relay is a switch your program can flip. It clicks on when its signal is HIGH, and a small light shows it's on.
grove-relay.legs: One Grove cable. Only use the screw terminals with a teacher: never connect mains power.
grove-relay.did_you_know: A relay uses a tiny electromagnet to pull a switch closed, so a small signal can switch a bigger circuit.

grove-buzzer.name: Grove Buzzer
grove-buzzer.what: A buzzer makes beeps and simple tunes. Your program chooses the note.
grove-buzzer.legs: One Grove cable into a digital port.
grove-buzzer.did_you_know: The buzzer has a thin disc inside that bends back and forth thousands of times a second to make sound.
